outcomes.text: Describe how and why the model of the atom has changed over time.
Describe the atom as a small positive nucleus holding nearly all the mass, surrounded by electrons.
Recall that atoms and small molecules are about 1 x 10^-10 m across.
Define density.
Explain density differences between solids, liquids and gases using particle arrangement.
Use density, mass and volume together, including when mass is conserved.
Describe how mass is conserved when a substance melts, freezes, evaporates, condenses or sublimates.
Explain that physical changes are reversible and the material recovers its properties, unlike chemical changes.
Describe how heating changes a system's stored energy, raising temperature or causing a change of state.
Define specific heat capacity and tell it apart from specific latent heat.
Calculate energy change from mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change.
Calculate energy change in a change of state from specific latent heat and mass.
Explain how gas molecule motion relates to the gas's temperature and pressure.
Explain how temperature affects gas pressure at constant volume.
Recall that gases compress and expand, and pressure gives a force at right angles to any surface.
Explain why increasing the volume of a gas at constant temperature lowers its pressure.
Explain how doing work on a gas raises its temperature.
Describe a simple model of the Earth's atmosphere and atmospheric pressure.
Explain why atmospheric pressure falls with height above the surface.
Describe the factors that influence floating and sinking.
Explain why liquid pressure rises with depth and density, giving an upward force on submerged objects.
Calculate pressure differences at different depths in a liquid.
Describe how to measure distance and time in different situations.
Measure distance and time, including from graphs, to calculate speed.
Convert units and compute rates using ratios and proportional reasoning.
Explain the vector-scalar difference for displacement and distance, velocity and speed.
Relate motion to distance-time and velocity-time graphs, reading lines and slopes.
Interpret the area enclosed under a velocity-time graph.
Calculate average speed for non-uniform motion.
Apply distance, time and speed formulae to uniform motion and uniform acceleration.
Recall ways objects interact: electrostatics, gravity, magnetism and contact forces including friction.
Describe how interactions come in pairs that put a force on each object.
Represent forces as vectors using free body diagrams.
Apply Newton's first law to objects moving at uniform velocity or changing speed or direction.
Use vector diagrams for resolving forces, resultant force and equilibrium.
Describe forces on an isolated object or system, including terminal velocity.
Use free body diagrams to show forces giving a resultant force.
Use free body diagrams to show balanced forces giving zero resultant force.
Apply Newton's second law to forces, masses and accelerations.
Explain inertia and define inertial mass as the ratio of force to acceleration.
Define momentum and describe it in collisions.
Apply formulae linking force, mass, velocity and acceleration to show how changes relate.
Use work done, force and distance, and describe the energy transfer.
Calculate stored energy and energy transfers, converting newton-metres to joules.
Explain power as the rate of energy transfer, with examples.
Recall and apply Newton's third law in equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations.
Explain why constant-speed circular motion means changing velocity.
Explain that stretching, bending or compressing an object needs more than one force.
Describe elastic and plastic deformation.
Describe the relationship between force and extension for a spring.
Tell linear from non-linear force-extension relationships.
Calculate a spring constant in linear cases.
Calculate the work done in stretching a spring.
Describe how all matter has a gravitational field, stronger for massive objects.
Define weight, how it is measured, and its link to gravitational field strength g.
Recall the acceleration in free fall.
Apply formulae linking force, mass and g.
Describe examples where forces cause rotation.
Define and calculate the moment of a force, including balanced objects.
Explain how levers and gears transmit the turning effect of forces.
Recall that fluid pressure gives a net force at right angles to any surface.
Use force, pressure and area in calculations, including simple hydraulic systems.
Describe charge as a property of all matter, positive or negative.
Describe how rubbing produces static electricity and sparks, and forces between charged objects.
Explain static electricity by transfer of electrons between objects.
Explain electric fields and how they help explain static electricity.
Recall that current is the rate of flow of charge and what is needed for charge to flow.
Recall that current is the same everywhere in a single closed loop.
Use the relationship between charge, current and time.
Describe differences between series and parallel circuits.
Draw d.c. circuits using standard terminals and symbols.
Recall how current depends on resistance and potential difference, and their units.
Recall and apply the relationship between current, resistance and potential difference.
Explain that some resistors keep constant resistance while others change with current.
Explain the design and use of circuits to explore these effects.
Use graphs to tell whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear.
Relate graph curves to the function and properties of circuit elements.
Explain why series resistors increase net resistance and parallel resistors decrease it.
Calculate currents, potential differences and resistances in series and parallel circuits.
Explain the design and use of d.c. circuits for measurement and testing.
Explain how power in a device relates to potential difference, current and energy changes over time.
Apply the equations for potential difference, current, charge, resistance, power, energy and time to circuit problems.

units.title: Topic P4: Magnetism and magnetic fields

outcomes.text: Describe attraction and repulsion between like and unlike poles of permanent magnets.
Describe the difference between permanent and induced magnets.
Describe a magnet's field, showing how strength and direction change from point to point.
Explain how a dipping compass is evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic.
Describe how a current creates a magnetic effect and the field direction around a wire.
Recall that field strength depends on current and distance from the conductor.
Explain how solenoids strengthen the magnetic effect.
Describe how a magnet and a current-carrying conductor exert a force on each other.
Show Fleming's left-hand rule relates force, current and magnetic field.
Apply the equation linking force on a conductor to flux density, current and length.
Explain how the force on a current-carrying conductor turns an electric motor.
Recall that a changing magnetic field around a conductor induces a potential difference that can drive a current.
Explain how this effect works in an alternator for a.c. and a dynamo for d.c.
Explain how an alternating current in one circuit induces a current in another, as in transformers.
Explain how the ratio of potential differences depends on the ratio of turns in the coils.
Apply the equations linking potential differences and turns in transformer coils.
Explain how a microphone turns sound pressure variations into current, and the reverse in a loudspeaker.
Describe wave motion using amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period.
Define wavelength and frequency.
Describe and apply the relationship between wavelength, frequency and wave velocity.
Apply formulae relating velocity, frequency and wavelength.
Describe the differences between transverse and longitudinal waves.
Describe how water ripples model transverse waves and sound is longitudinal, and how their speeds are measured.
Describe evidence that the wave travels, not the water or air.
Show how velocity, frequency and wavelength change when sound passes between media.
Describe reflection, transmission and absorption of waves at material boundaries.
Describe processes that convert sound waves to vibrations in solids and back.
Explain why such processes work only over a limited frequency range, linked to human hearing.
Recall that electromagnetic waves are transverse and all travel at the same velocity through space.
Explain that electromagnetic waves transfer energy from source to absorber.
Apply the relationship between frequency and wavelength across the spectrum.
Describe the main groups of the spectrum, from long to short wavelength and low to high frequency.
Describe that eyes detect only a limited range of the spectrum.
Recall that light is an electromagnetic wave.
Give practical uses of radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma waves.
Describe how ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays can harm body tissue.
Explain how differences in wave velocity, absorption and reflection allow detection and exploration of solids and liquids.
Recall that radio waves can be produced by, or induce, oscillations in electrical circuits.
Recall that substances absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves depending on wavelength.
Explain how some effects relate to different wave velocities in different substances.
Use ray diagrams for reflection and refraction, including convex and concave lenses.
Construct two-dimensional ray diagrams of reflection and refraction, qualitatively.
Explain how colour relates to differential absorption, transmission and reflection.
Recall that nuclei contain protons and neutrons, and each element's nucleus has a characteristic positive charge.
Recall that atoms of one element can differ in neutron number, giving isotopes.
Use nuclear notation to relate the identities, charges and masses of isotopes.
Recall that unstable nuclei may emit alpha, beta, neutrons or gamma radiation.
Relate each emission to changes in the nucleus's mass or charge.
Use nuclear symbols to write equations for radioactive decay.
Balance decay equations for alpha, beta or gamma emission in mass and charge.
Recall that electron arrangements change on absorbing or emitting radiation.
Recall that changes in atoms and nuclei generate and absorb radiation over a wide frequency range.
Explain half-life and its link to the random nature of decay.
Calculate the decline, as a ratio, after a whole number of half-lives.
Recall how penetration differs for alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays.
Tell contamination from irradiation and compare their hazards.
Explain why hazards depend on the half-life of the material.
Describe uses of radiation for exploring internal organs and controlling or destroying tissue.
Recall that some nuclei split, and relate this to emitted radiation, energy transfer and chain reactions.
Describe nuclear fusion and that mass may convert to radiation energy.
Describe that total energy in a closed system does not change when it is transferred.
Describe all changes in how energy is stored in common situations.
Describe energy changes from heating and from work done by forces.
Calculate energy changes in a system, choosing mechanical, electrical or thermal equations.
Calculate energy of a moving body, a stretched spring and an object raised above ground.
Describe how energy is dissipated into less useful stores, with examples.
Describe energy transfers in domestic devices and how energy is wasted.
Describe how appliance power ratings link to energy transfer.
Calculate energy efficiency for any energy transfer.
Describe ways to increase efficiency.
Explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfer, such as lubrication and insulation.
Describe how a building's rate of cooling depends on wall thickness and thermal conductivity.
Recall typical speeds of wind, sound and everyday transport.
Estimate the size of everyday accelerations.
Convert units and compute rates using ratios.
Explain how human reaction times are measured and recall typical results.
Explain factors affecting a vehicle's stopping distance and the safety implications.
Estimate how stopping distances vary with speed.
Explain the dangers of large decelerations.
Estimate forces in typical situations on a public road.
Estimate speed, acceleration and forces in large accelerations of road transport.
Describe the main energy sources on Earth, compare their use, and tell renewable from non-renewable.
Explain patterns and trends in energy resource use over time.
Recall that grid power moves at high voltage and is stepped down for local use.
Recall that step-up and step-down transformers change potential difference along the grid.
Explain why the national grid is an efficient way to transfer energy.
Link transformer turns and potential differences to power transfer and the advantage of high-voltage transmission.
Recall that UK mains is a.c. at 50 Hz and about 230 V.
Explain the difference between direct and alternating voltage.
Recall the functions of live, neutral and earth wires and the potential differences between them.
Explain why a live wire can be dangerous with an open switch, and the dangers of connecting it to earth.
Explain red-shift of light from receding galaxies.
Explain how red-shift and other evidence link to the Big Bang model.
Recall that the Sun formed from dust and gas drawn by gravity, with fusion balancing gravity.
Explain that all bodies emit radiation depending on temperature.
Recall the main features of the solar system, planets, moons and artificial satellites.
Explain how gravity changes a planet's velocity but not its speed in a circular orbit.
Explain how a stable orbit's radius must change if speed changes.
Explain how a body's temperature depends on balance between radiation absorbed and emitted.
Explain how wave velocity, absorption and reflection differences allow detection and exploration.
